```{r setup}
library(lab6)
```

## The data

All examples use `knapsack_objects`, a data.frame of 2000 randomly generated
objects, each with a weight `w` and a value `v`, generated with a fixed seed 
so results are reproducible.

```{r}
head(knapsack_objects)
nrow(knapsack_objects)
```

## Brute force search

`brute_force_knapsack()` finds the exact optimal solution by checking every
possible subset of the objects. Its running time is O(2^n), so it is only 
practical for small n.

```{r}
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 3500)
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:12, ], W = 3500)
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 2000)
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:12, ], W = 2000)
```

**Question: how much time does it take to run the algorithm for n = 16
objects?**

```{r}
system.time(brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:16, ], W = 3500))
```

## Dynamic programming

`knapsack_dynamic()` finds the same exact solution using dynamic programming.
Since the weights are integers, the running time is O(W * n), which scales far 
better than brute force for larger n.

```{r}
knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 3500)
knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:12, ], W = 3500)
knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 2000)
knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:12, ], W = 2000)
```

**Question: how much time does it take to run the algorithm for 
n = 500 objects?**

```{r}
system.time(knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500))
```

## Profiling and optimizing knapsack_dynamic()

Profiling `knapsack_dynamic()` with `profvis` showed that most of the time 
was spent in the inner loop, which filled the dynamic programming table one
cell at a time. The inner loop was rewritten to update an entire table row
at once using `pmax()`, avoiding per-cell indexing.

The code below reproduces the original, unvectorized inner loop locally for 
comparison, and times it against the current, vectorized implementation on the
same input.

```{r}
knapsack_dynamic_naive <- function(x, W) {
  n <- nrow(x)
  Wcap <- floor(W)
  m <- matrix(0, nrow = n + 1, ncol = Wcap + 1)
  
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    wi <- x$w[i]
    vi <- x$v[i]
    for (w in 0:Wcap) {
      if (wi > w) {
        m[i + 1, w + 1] <- m[i, w + 1]
      }
      else {
        m[i + 1, w + 1] <- max(m[i, w + 1], m[i, w - wi + 1] + vi)
      }
    }
  }
  m[n + 1, Wcap + 1]
}

t_naive <- system.time(knapsack_dynamic_naive(x = knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500))
t_fast <- system.time(knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500))

t_naive
t_fast
```

**Question: what performance gain could you get by trying to improve your 
code?**

```{r}
as.numeric(t_naive["elapsed"]) / as.numeric(t_fast["elapsed"])
```

## Greedy heuristic
`greedy_knapsack()` sorts the objects by value per unit weight and adds
them in that order, stopping as soon as an object no longer fits. this does not
guarantee an optimal solution but it is guaranteed to return at least 50% of 
the true maximum value, and runs in O(nlogn).

```{r}
greedy_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:800, ], W = 3500)
greedy_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:1200, ], W = 3500)
```

**Question: how much time does it take to run the algorithm for n = 1 000 000
objects?**

```{r}
set.seed(1)
n_big <- 1000000
big_objects <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, size = n_big, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(n_big, 0, 10000)
)

system.time(greedy_knapsack(x = big_objects, W = 3500))
```

## Parallelizing brute force search
`brute_force_knapsack()` accepts a `parallel` argument. When `True`, the search
space is split into one chunk per detected CPU core, searched independently
with `parallel::makeCluster()`, and the best result acros chunks is returned.

```{r}
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:16, ], W = 3500)
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:16, ], W = 3500, parallel = TRUE)
```

**Question: what performance gain could you get by parallelizing brute force 
search?**

```{r}
t_seq <- system.time(brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:20, ], W = 3500))
t_par <- system.time(brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:20, ], W = 3500, parallel = TRUE))

t_seq
t_par
as.numeric(t_seq["elapsed"]) / as.numeric(t_par["elapsed"])
```

The speedup is smaller than the number of detected cores would suggest,
since starting the cluster and copying data to each worker process adds
overhead that does not shrink proportionally with the search space.
